dmm-2009-power-01.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. How many rotationally distinct colorings of the faces of a cube with the colors white and black are there?

dmm-2009-power-02a.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Pick a face of the cube and call it $A$. Consider rotations of the cube into itself (the rotation that does not move the cube at all always counts as a rotation). How many such rotations take face $A$ to itself?

dmm-2009-power-02b.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Pick a face $A$ and another face $B$. Count the number of rotations of the cube into itself that move $A$ to $B$. Explain why this answer is the same as the number of rotations that take $A$ to itself, by giving a way to match up the two sets of rotations.

dmm-2009-power-02c.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Count the total number of rotations of a cube into itself.

dmm-2009-power-03a.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Consider the coloring of a cube obtained by wrapping the diagram into a cube (the shaded squares are black, the other squares are white: the horizontal row has the pattern black, black, white, black, and the two squares above and below the third square are white). Count the number of rotations of the cube into itself that do not change the color of any face (rotations that take black faces to black faces and white faces to white faces).

dmm-2009-power-03b.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Consider the cube colored as in the previous part (three black faces: left, back, right; three white faces: front, top, bottom). Using the number of rotations of the cube (24) and the number of color-preserving rotations (2), count the number of colorings that are rotationally equivalent to this cube, i.e. the number of colorings that can be formed by rotating this cube.

dmm-2009-power-04a.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Let $N$ be the number of rotationally distinct colorings of a cube with $10$ colors. For each rotation $r$ of the cube into itself, let $\mathrm{Fix}(r)$ be the number of colorings $c$ (not necessarily rotationally distinct) that $r$ leaves unchanged. Consider all ordered pairs $(r,c)$ in which rotation $r$ leaves coloring $c$ unchanged. Count the number of all such ordered pairs, expressing the answer using the function $\mathrm{Fix}$.

dmm-2009-power-05a.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Let $N$ be the number of rotationally distinct colorings of a cube with $10$ colors, and consider the ordered pairs $(r,c)$ in which the rotation $r$ leaves the coloring $c$ unchanged. Count these pairs by fixing the coloring first, and express the answer in terms of $N$. (Use the ideas of the previous problems: if a coloring $c$ has $t$ rotations leaving it unchanged, then exactly $24/t$ colorings are rotationally equivalent to $c$.)

dmm-2009-power-05b.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Let $N$ be the number of rotationally distinct colorings of a cube with $10$ colors. Prove that $N$ is the average of $\mathrm{Fix}(r)$ over all rotations $r$.

dmm-2009-power-06a.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Two rotations are of the same *type* if they do the same thing except possibly to different faces and in possibly different orientations. For instance all $90^\circ$ rotations about a face are of the same type, all $180^\circ$ rotations about a face are of the same type. Completely classify all rotations of the cube into types, and count the number of rotations of each type.

dmm-2009-power-06b.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Explain why, if rotation $r_1$ and rotation $r_2$ are of the same type, then $\mathrm{Fix}(r_1)=\mathrm{Fix}(r_2)$ (where $\mathrm{Fix}(r)$ is the number of colorings, with a given set of colors, unchanged by $r$).

dmm-2009-power-06c.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Compute $\mathrm{Fix}(r)$ for each type of rotation, where colorings use $10$ colors. ($\mathrm{Fix}(r)$ is the number of colorings, not necessarily rotationally distinct, that the rotation $r$ leaves unchanged.)

dmm-2009-power-07.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Using the classification of rotations of the cube and the formula $N=\frac1{24}\sum_r\mathrm{Fix}(r)$, find $N$: the number of rotationally distinct colorings of a cube using $10$ colors. (Rotation types: identity $1$ rotation with $10^6$ fixed colorings; $90^\circ$/$270^\circ$ face rotations $6$ with $10^3$; $180^\circ$ face rotations $3$ with $10^4$; vertex rotations $8$ with $10^2$; edge rotations $6$ with $10^3$.)

dmm-2009-power-08.prompt: Consider the faces of a cube. A *coloring* assigns a color to each of the six faces. Two colorings are *rotationally equivalent* if one can be rotated into the other; otherwise they are *rotationally distinct*. Express the number of rotationally distinct colorings of a cube using $n$ colors in terms of $n$.

dmm-2009-power-09.prompt: Two colorings of the faces of a regular tetrahedron are rotationally equivalent if one can be rotated into the other. Find, in terms of $n$, the number of rotationally distinct colorings of the faces of a regular tetrahedron using $n$ colors.
